Non-normative. Nothing in this section is a requirement; [§4](#4-key-material) and [§7](#7-operations) already say everything required about keys and signatures regardless of who holds them. This section exists because [§10](#10-security-considerations)'s custody-disclosure point and [§12.1](#121-the-three-authorities)'s "control" authority both read differently depending on which of two shapes actually holds for a given identity's operational key:

- **Registrar-held**: the registrar generated the operational key and still holds it, encrypted, able to sign ordinary rotations and other self-contained operations on the ward's behalf via whatever login mechanism it offers. Nothing about the method distinguishes this from any other client holding a key -- the registrar is simply acting as the key-holding client here, not exercising some separate, method-level authority. Convenient, and the only shape self-service registration produces. The registrar's trustworthiness is now part of what "control" rests on for that identity, not just naming and currency.
- **Self-held**: the ward holds its operational key, and the registrar holds nothing usable -- not even an encrypted copy. A registrar offering a transition from the first shape to the second, after registration, is documented as "take-custody" in the registrar API specification; nothing here requires a registrar to offer it, and this document defines no new operation type for it, since the result is an ordinary guardian- or ward-signed `custodial_rotate` either way.

Neither shape changes which signatures [§7](#7-operations) requires -- it only changes who is capable of producing the ward's half of them, and who a verifier is trusting when a registrar's convenience endpoint produces a signature "on a ward's behalf."

## Method and registrar profile

Everything normative in [§1](#1-target-system) through [§12](#12-authority-and-trust-model) is **the method**: what any conformant registrar must do, and what any verifier can check against any conformant registrar, regardless of implementation. Concretely:

- a hash-chained log whose genesis is self-signed by its declared keys (REQ-7.1-8) and attested by the accepting registrar (REQ-7.1-5)
- operations signed according to the signer formulas [§7](#7-operations) states, governed by `GuardianPolicy`
- registrar ordering, plus signed, timestamped heads (REQ-12-1's L2)
- `GET` the document, the log, and the log head; `POST` one signed operation, including genesis (REQ-8-2)
- optional guardianship -- a ward works the same with or without one, at genesis or afterward

Everything else -- sessions, `/register` with server-side key generation, OIDC login, email-based account recovery, the asynchronous propose/sign-individual flow, `take-custody`, the Managed Identity API, A2A/MCP integration, cross-registrar relay -- is **registrar profile**: this reference registrar's operational choices, fully documented in the [registrar API specification](/docs/registrar/), which labels itself exactly that way. A different registrar is free to offer none of it, some other convenience surface entirely, or the bare method-required endpoints alone, and remain just as conformant. Where this document describes registrar-profile behavior at all (the examples above, [§12.4](#124-key-custody-modes)'s custody modes), it's a non-normative pointer to help a reader place it, never a requirement.

## Conformance

A conformant implementation must replay and verify every fixture in [`interop_tests/`](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/tree/main/interop_tests) the same way this reference implementation does -- accepting every fixture whose own `expect` is `accept`, rejecting every one whose `expect` is `reject`, each for the specific reason its own `note` states. [`requirements.json`](https://guardianspec.org/requirements.json) lists every requirement in this document by id, cross-referenced with the reference implementation's own tests that name it. [JSON Schemas](https://guardianspec.org/schemas/operation.schema.json) for `GuardianPolicy` and every operation type are also available, matching this document's own field-by-field requirements.

**Accept:**

- `genesis_two_guardians.json`: Genesis establishing a two-member guardian set, both consenting.
- `guardian_relinquish_unanimous.json`: Both guardians sign off on full relinquishment -- meets the default majority (here, unanimous since n=2) threshold.
- `rotate_then_guardian_add_remove.json`: Genesis, an ordinary operational-key rotation, then board-a steps down (voluntary `guardian_remove`) and board-c joins (`guardian_add`, needing board-b's own continuing approval) -- board-b itself is never removed or re-added.
- `tombstone_any_single_key.json`: Guardian-less ward tombstoning itself via its own operational key (resolved under its own DID), meeting the default `any` tombstone_threshold.
- `guardian_add_zero_to_one.json`: A standalone `guardian_add` establishing the first guardian for a previously guardian-less ward, with both the incoming guardian's and the ward's signatures present (REQ-7.2-5).
- `root_genesis_self_attestation.json`: the bare-domain root identity's own genesis, attested only by its own proof of possession -- no separate registrar attestation exists or is needed (Fix 7, REQ-7.1-5).

**Reject:**

- `forged_guardian_claim.json`: 'board-a' is named as initial guardian but the proof was produced by a different, impostor key -- must fail verification against board-a's own resolved public key.
- `relinquish_quorum_not_met.json`: three guardians exist, default removal/relinquish threshold is majority (2 of 3), but only board-a signed.
- `unilateral_coguardian_removal.json`: troy attempts to remove jane from a two-guardian set, but the proof claimed as jane's was produced with troy's own key, not jane's.
- `genesis_missing_registrar_attestation.json`: a genesis operation with no registrar attestation at all -- must fail REQ-7.1-5, not just a forged one.
- `genesis_unsigned_incoming_guardian.json`: 'board-a' is named as an incoming guardian directly at genesis but carries no proof at all -- must fail REQ-7.1-1.
- `guardian_add_missing_ward_signature.json`: a standalone `guardian_add` naming 'board-a' is signed by board-a alone -- the ward's required signature (REQ-7.2-5) is missing.
- `genesis_pop_key_mismatch.json`: `operationalKeys` names a key the submitter does not hold -- the only proof of possession attached is for a different key the submitter actually controls (Fix 1, REQ-7.1-8).
- `policy_version_gate_blocks_governed_op.json`: an otherwise fully and validly signed `guardian_add`, governed by a `GuardianPolicy` whose `version` exceeds what this verifier understands -- must be refused regardless (Fix 6, REQ-5-9).

## Changelog

- **v0.2.0** (2026-10-24, current): domain-first identifier grammar (`did:guardian:<domain>:<name>`, matching `did:web`'s own convention); the bare-domain identity as a first-class concept ([§2.1](#21-the-bare-domain-identity)); the nullification window ([REQ-6-9](#req-6-9)); every requirement given a stable `REQ-<section>-<n>` id.
  - **2026-11-22**: five more spec-design gaps from the same external review, resolved per the user's own earlier decisions on each: added [REQ-5-10](#req-5-10) -- an unset `GuardianPolicy` field resolves to this document's own stated default only, never a registrar-configured one, and simplified [REQ-7.1-5](#req-7.1-5)/genesis-policy's wording ([REQ-7.1-7](#req-7.1-7)) to match (an earlier version of REQ-7.1-7 allowed a registrar-configured override at genesis specifically, contradicting the general rule this entry now states). Tightened [REQ-7.1-5](#req-7.1-5): the registrar DID a genesis attestation is checked against is now explicitly `did:guardian:<domain-of-did>`, structurally derived from `did` the same way [REQ-7.1-10](#req-7.1-10) already does, never read from the proof's own `verificationMethod` as an independently-trusted value (already true of the reference implementation's `expectedRegistrarDid`; this entry states it normatively). Added a root-identity lifecycle paragraph to [§2.1](#21-the-bare-domain-identity) covering bootstrap (self-attestation, Fix 7), rotation (an ordinary `custodial_rotate`, point-in-time key resolution per [REQ-4-2](#req-4-2) applying to a registrar-as-signer same as a guardian-as-signer), and tombstone (blocks *new* genesis acceptance under that domain without retroactively un-attesting anything already signed). Clarified [REQ-5-1](#req-5-1): `N`/`M` count distinct signer DIDs, never raw signatures or keys -- a ward presenting more than one operational key still counts as exactly one member of a union-based eligible set (already true of `quorum.ts`'s own `Set`-based counting; stated normatively). Added two [§10](#10-security-considerations) entries: cross-registrar guardian history (a guardian hosted elsewhere transitively imports that registrar's own trust properties, deliberately left unrestricted rather than add a same-registrar-only rule with its own edge cases) and name non-reuse ([REQ-9-2](#req-9-2)) relying on registrar honesty, detectable the same way domain takeover already is -- a pinned anchor from first contact ([REQ-12-2](#req-12-2)) catching a later resolution under the same `domain:name` returning a different log entirely.
  - **2026-11-22**: [REQ-8-2](#req-8-2) now requires a log-head endpoint from every conformant registrar -- [L2](#122-verification-levels) freshness moves from a reference-registrar convenience to a method requirement, closing the gap where [Method and registrar profile](#method-and-registrar-profile)'s own summary already described it that way while the requirement's actual text hadn't caught up. The log-head statement's `sig` field (raw base64url, the one signature in this method that didn't follow [REQ-6-7](#req-6-7)'s own format) is replaced with `proof`, a single [W3C Data Integrity](https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-integrity/) proof -- never an array, since a log-head statement has exactly one signer by construction. Also stated explicitly what the implementation already did: `seq` counts every entry the full stored log holds, superseded branches included, not just the currently-active chain, so it only ever grows. The reference library's `signLogHeadStatement`/`verifyLogHeadStatement` now use the same `createProof`/`verifyAgainstKeys` machinery every other signature in this method already uses, instead of the separate `signPayload`/`verifyPayload` raw scheme.
  - **2026-11-21**: a coordinated security rewrite, following an external review of this version's own proof-of-possession/registrar-attestation work above. Seven fixes, implemented together since several touch the same signed content:
    - **Fix 1 -- operational-key proof-of-possession, tightened ([REQ-7.1-8](#req-7.1-8)/[REQ-7.2-12](#req-7.2-12))**: the prior `verificationMethods` map (a separate, DID-indexed list of presented keys) is removed entirely -- a DID Document's `verificationMethod` entries are now derived directly from `operationalKeys` by position, with nothing else to desync from it. More importantly, proof-of-possession verification now checks that each operational key has its OWN matching proof, rather than merely that some valid proof exists somewhere in the set -- closing a real gap where an attacker could present a victim's key in the document while actually controlling, and only ever proving possession of, a different key.
    - **Fix 2 -- genesis bound to its own domain ([REQ-7.1-10](#req-7.1-10))**: genesis now carries a required `did` field, and a registrar must reject any genesis whose `did` doesn't match the identity it would actually create under that registrar's own domain. Closes cross-registrar genesis replay: before this, a public genesis accepted at one registrar carried no cryptographic link to where it was meant to live, and could be resubmitted verbatim at a different registrar under the same free name.
    - **Fix 3 -- deterministic, malleability-resistant anchors ([REQ-6-4](#req-6-4))**: a cid is now computed with every proof stripped from the content first, rather than over the full signed operation -- making it independent of which signature happened to be produced, and computable by a client before submission. Paired with this, ECDSA signing/verification now rejects (not merely avoids producing) a signature's high-S, equally-valid-but-malleable counterpart, so a given (message, key) pair has exactly one valid signature, bit for bit.
    - **Fix 4 -- canonicalization and wire format, unified**: serialization moves from DAG-CBOR to [JCS (RFC 8785)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785); every cid becomes a sha2-256 [multihash](https://github.com/multiformats/multihash), base58btc-encoded with a leading `z`; every public key, everywhere this method presents one, becomes a [Multikey](https://www.w3.org/TR/cid-1.0/#Multikey) -- the earlier base64url SPKI format is now purely an internal implementation detail at the WebCrypto import/export boundary, never part of this method's own wire format.
    - **Fix 5 -- the signed envelope replaced with W3C Data Integrity proofs ([REQ-6-7](#req-6-7))**: the `sig`/`sigs`/`keySigs`/`registrar` fields are retired in favor of one `proof` array of [W3C Data Integrity](https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-integrity/) proofs (`ecdsa-jcs-2019`), each proof naming its own signer via `verificationMethod` instead of being keyed externally by DID or raw key string. The registrar's own genesis attestation is now just one more proof in the same array, rather than a separately-shaped field -- see Fix 7 below for the one case where it's absent by design. Because a proof's own `created` timestamp sits outside the (proof-stripped) anchor content, the [L2](#122-verification-levels) log-head statement gains a required `logHash` field separately committing to the full log including every proof, closing the gap where a registrar could otherwise re-sign an identical entry under a different `created` undetected.
    - **Fix 6 -- `GuardianPolicy` versioning replaces "ignore unknown fields" ([REQ-5-9](#req-5-9))**: the previous rule (a verifier ignores any policy field it doesn't recognize) is replaced with an explicit `version` field and a hard refusal: a verifier encountering a policy version newer than it understands must refuse to evaluate ANY operation that policy governs, not just skip the one field it can't parse. The earlier rule was a silent downgrade risk -- ignoring an unrecognized field gives no way to tell whether some OTHER, more restrictive unrecognized field was also supposed to apply to that same decision.
    - **Fix 7 -- root genesis self-attestation ([REQ-7.1-5](#req-7.1-5))**: the bare-domain root identity's own genesis is now explicitly accepted with no separate registrar attestation, since its own required proof of possession already is the only attestation possible for the one identity a deployment bootstraps on its own -- there is no other party on that deployment to vouch for it. Implemented as a narrow exception (`did === registrarDid`) inside genesis verification, not a general carve-out.

      Together these replace every `signCustodialCreate`/`verifyCustodialCreate`/`signCustodialRotate`/`verifyCustodialRotate`/`signGuardianAdd`/`signGuardianRemove`/`signPolicyUpdate`/`signGuardianRelinquish`/`signCustodialTombstone` function in the reference library, the reference registrar's full acceptance path (including its asynchronous multi-signer pending-operations machinery) and its cross-registrar signature relay, and every command in `@did-guardian/cli` that builds or submits an operation. Every interop fixture was regenerated from the reference implementation itself (never hand-edited), plus two new ones specifically exercising Fix 1 (`genesis_pop_key_mismatch.json`) and Fix 6 (`policy_version_gate_blocks_governed_op.json`), and a new accept fixture for Fix 7 (`root_genesis_self_attestation.json`).
  - **2026-11-21**: added [Method and registrar profile](#method-and-registrar-profile), drawing an explicit boundary between what every conformant registrar must do and this reference registrar's operational choices -- prompted by this version's own steps blurring that line in places (genesis submission moving into the method itself, custody modes touching on registrar behavior). The registrar API spec now labels itself a registrar profile, not the method, and [§12.4](#124-key-custody-modes) says plainly that a registrar holding a ward's key is acting as that ward's key-holding client, not exercising a separate method-level authority.
  - **2026-11-21**: relaxed [REQ-7.1-1](#req-7.1-1) -- `incoming` may now name one or more guardians directly at genesis, as long as each co-signs, instead of always being `[]`. Removes the "self-held identities are always born guardian-less" trap, and halves the operations an identity that's always born with a guardian needs (an ephemeral agent fleet under one long-lived guardian, say). Added [REQ-7.1-9](#req-7.1-9): a ward can't name itself as a guardian at genesis either, same reasoning as [REQ-7.2-11](#req-7.2-11). `checkGenesisShape` (`rules.ts`) is wired into the reference registrar's `acceptGenesis` now rather than standing alone as a tested-but-unused function, and checks the new rule's shape (a signature slot exists for each named guardian); genesis's cryptographic checks (those signatures' validity, keySigs, the registrar attestation) still run through `verifyCustodialCreate`, called once the attestation is attached. `@did-guardian/cli`'s `create --guardian <did> --guardian-key <label>` covers the case where the same operator holds both keys. New interop fixtures: a genesis naming an incoming guardian with no signature at all is rejected; one where each named guardian co-signs is accepted (the latter was already covered by an existing fixture, since `verifyCustodialCreate` never actually required `incoming` to be empty -- only this requirement's own wording and the unwired shape check did).
  - **2026-11-21**: amended [REQ-8-2](#req-8-2) -- genesis submission is part of the method now, not a registrar-specific convenience. `POST .../operations` at a name this registrar doesn't yet host accepts a self-signed `custodial_create`, checked for name validity/availability and proof of possession, with the registrar's attestation added before storing it. The reference registrar's `registerWard` (server-generated key) now goes through this exact same acceptance path (`acceptGenesis`, registrar.ts) a client-built genesis does -- one creation path, two kinds of callers. `@did-guardian/cli`'s `create --registrar <domain>` publishes for real now and reports the registrar's returned anchor as the confirmed value for convenience. (Corrected 2026-11-22: per [REQ-6-4](#req-6-4), every proof is stripped before hashing, so this anchor is identical to the one computed locally before the attestation existed -- the attestation never changes it. An earlier version of this entry claimed otherwise; [WS-3.7 audit fix](#changelog) corrected the CLI's own labels to match.) This resolves [issue #4](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/issues/4).
  - **2026-11-21**: added [REQ-7.1-8](#req-7.1-8) -- genesis now requires `keySigs` (a field name this same day's later [Fix 5 rewrite above](#changelog) retires in favor of the unified `proof` array; this entry records the requirement's own origin, not its current wire shape), a proof-of-possession signature from every declared operational key, closing the gap where the control chain's root was whatever the registrar's naming attestation asserted, with nothing self-certifying behind it. Generalized the same requirement to `custodial_rotate` as [REQ-7.2-12](#req-7.2-12): any operation that installs a new key carries that key's proof of possession, not just the signature authorizing the change. The reference library's `signCustodialCreate`/`verifyCustodialCreate`/`signCustodialRotate`/`verifyCustodialRotate` (all four, themselves later retired by [Fix 5](#changelog) in favor of the current proof-model functions) and the real server-side `rotateRule` (`rules.ts`) all checked it; every interop fixture was regenerated to match.
  - **2026-11-19**: implemented [L2](#122-verification-levels) (REQ-12-1) -- the reference registrar now exposes a signed log-head statement at `.../log-head` (registrar API spec), using the same key as REQ-7.1-5's genesis attestation. Also added `multikeyToSpki` to the reference library (the inverse of `spkiToMultikey`), closing a real gap this surfaced: a verifier who only has a resolved DID document had no way to get back to this library's internal key format needed to check any signature at all. [Issue #5](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/issues/5) is now fully addressed by this and the REQ-12-4 work below.
  - **2026-11-19**: implemented [REQ-12-4](#req-12-4)'s anchor field on `guardian_add` -- the reference library's `GuardianAddOp` type, the reference registrar's same-registrar convenience paths, `@did-guardian/cli`'s `guardian add`, and the JSON Schema all carry it now. (Filed [issue #6](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/issues/6) while adding this: the `interop_tests/` conformance suite has no fixture exercising a standalone `guardian_add` at all, independent of the anchor field specifically.)
    - **2026-11-21**: closed [issue #6](https://github.com/did-method-guardian/did-method-guardian/issues/6). Added `guardian_add_zero_to_one.json` (accept) and `guardian_add_missing_ward_signature.json` (reject), and fixed the gap the issue's title undersold: `interop.test.ts`'s `verifyLog` harness had no case for `guardian_add`, `guardian_remove`, or `policy_update` at all -- any fixture exercising one would have silently passed regardless of whether its signatures were actually valid, since none of those types matched any branch and the loop just moved on. Now routed through `verifyByRules` (`rules.ts`), the same function the registrar uses, with the fixture's state replayed incrementally as of just before each entry.
  - **2026-11-18**: documented domain migration as explicitly out of scope for this version ([§9](#9-deactivation-and-data-permanence)), with "link, don't move" (a new identifier plus mutual `alsoKnownAs`) as the documented alternative. Added [§12, Authority and trust model](#12-authority-and-trust-model) -- the three authorities (control/naming/currency), verification levels L0-L3 and the first-contact-then-pin rule ([REQ-12-1](#req-12-1)/[REQ-12-2](#req-12-2)/[REQ-12-3](#req-12-3)), pinning ([REQ-12-4](#req-12-4)), and non-normative key custody modes ([§12.4](#124-key-custody-modes)). Reworded [REQ-6-3](#req-6-3) -- the anchor (genesis content hash) is a property of the log, not of the identifier, which was never actually hash-derived under this version's domain-first grammar. Tightened [REQ-7.1-5](#req-7.1-5) from `MAY` to `MUST`: every genesis now requires a registrar attestation, not just accepts one if present -- the reference library's `verifyCustodialCreate` function (later rewritten, same name retained, by [Fix 5](#changelog)'s proof-model migration) and every interop fixture were updated to match. Added security-considerations entries for log forgery/stale snapshots, domain takeover, equivocation, and custody disclosure.
- **v0.1** (2026-10-19 through 2026-10-23): initial draft, before the method specification, registrar API, and guide were split into separate documents. Never published as its own standalone page.


---

# did:guardian Registrar API, v1 (the reference registrar)

Canonical URL: https://guardianspec.org/docs/registrar/

**Version 1.** This document is a registrar profile, not the method: exactly one registrar implementation's HTTP surface -- `packages/server` in this repository, deployed as guardianspec.org's registrar. It is versioned and evolves independently of [the formal method specification](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/) -- adding, removing, or reshaping anything here never changes method conformance, and a different registrar implementation is free to expose none of it. Only [§1](#1-method-required-endpoints) restates an actual method requirement; everything else is this registrar's own operational choice. See the method spec's [Method and registrar profile](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#method-and-registrar-profile) section for exactly where that line is drawn.

All endpoints are rooted at `/.well-known/guardian/<name>` (or `/.well-known/guardian/_` for the bare-domain identity). All request/response bodies are JSON unless noted.

## 1. Method-required endpoints

Required by the formal spec's REQ-8-2; this registrar's own implementation of them.

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/.well-known/guardian/<name>` | current derived DID Document |
| `GET` | `/.well-known/guardian/<name>/log` | full operation log, timestamped |
| `GET` | `/.well-known/guardian/<name>/log-head` | a signed, timestamped statement about the current log head (spec §12.2, REQ-12-1's L2) |
| `POST` | `/.well-known/guardian/<name>/operations` | submit one fully-signed operation |

`POST .../operations` accepts any operation type from the formal spec's §7 with all required signatures already attached (per that operation's own REQ-7.x signer rules) and appends it if valid, rejecting with a reason string otherwise. This is the only path by which an *externally* pre-signed operation (e.g. two guardians who coordinated their own signatures out-of-band) reaches the log directly, without going through §3's collection machinery.

`.../log-head` exists to make L2 ("fresh as of t") achievable without a live round-trip every time -- a method requirement as of the spec's 2026-11-22 revision, not merely this registrar's own convenience. Computed and signed fresh on every call, never stored: `{did, anchor, headCid, seq, logHash, timestamp, registrar, proof}`, where `proof` is one [W3C Data Integrity](https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-integrity/) proof (never an array -- exactly one signer by construction), signed with the same root-identity key REQ-7.1-5's genesis attestation already uses. `logHash` separately commits to the full log, every entry's proofs included -- `headCid`/`anchor` deliberately exclude them, same as any other cid (spec [REQ-6-4](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-4)). `seq` is the log's full stored length, counting every entry a nullification ever superseded, not just the currently-active chain -- it only ever grows. A caller who holds this can show it to a third party later as evidence the log was at this exact head as of this exact time, without that third party needing to resolve this registrar at all -- the same role OCSP stapling plays for certificate revocation. Public, like the document and the log themselves: a signed claim about where a public log stands is exactly as safe to hand to anyone as the log is.

## 2. Self-contained convenience endpoints

Each of these corresponds to an operation whose formal signer requirement can be satisfied by a single call from one authenticated party, with this registrar producing every needed signature itself from keys it already custodies -- no new authority is ever granted to a third party by any of these, which is what makes a single bare call safe. Auth model, uniformly: either an active `gw_session` cookie for the target identity itself, or a trusted OIDC client credential (Basic auth) acting on an already-verified decision made by its own caller (e.g. zz, having already confirmed its own user is a current guardian, before ever calling here).

| Method | Path | Operation produced | Why it's self-contained |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `.../rotate` | `custodial_rotate`, ward-signed | self-rotation grants no new authority |
| `POST` | `.../take-custody` | `custodial_rotate` to a caller-supplied public key | signed with the key this registrar still custodies -- the last signature it ever produces for this identity -- plus the caller's proof of possession of the new key (REQ-7.2-12), which this registrar never holds and so can't produce |
| `POST` | `.../remove-self` | `guardian_remove`, voluntary (`outgoing = [caller]`) | needs only the caller's own consent (REQ-7.2-7a) |
| `POST` | `.../remove` | `guardian_remove`, forced | self-contained **only** when the *other* current guardians (excluding the one being removed) are custodied entirely by this registrar **and** that custodied subset alone meets `removal_threshold` (REQ-7.2-7b); otherwise rejected, directing the caller to §3 |
| `POST` | `.../relinquish` | `guardian_relinquish` | self-contained **only** when the current guardian set is custodied entirely by this registrar **and** that custodied subset alone meets `removal_threshold` (e.g. a sole guardian, trivially); otherwise rejected with a clear reason directing the caller to §3 |
| `POST` | `.../tombstone` | `custodial_tombstone`, ward-signed | `tombstone_threshold` defaults to `any`; the ward's own key alone always suffices. If the identity is itself a current guardian of anything, see §4's own acceptance/cascade policy first |
| `POST` | `.../adopt` | `guardian_add`, zero-to-one case only | needs only the incoming party's own consent plus the ward's own key (REQ-7.2-5) -- rejected if the ward already has any current guardian; use §3 for a non-empty guardian set |

**`.../take-custody` is irreversible in a way nothing else on this page is.** Every other row above produces an operation and nothing changes about who's custodied going forward. This one ends it: body `{public_key, key_proof, force?}`. `key_proof` is a [W3C Data Integrity proof](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-7) -- a self-contained `did:key:<public_key>#<public_key>` proof of possession -- built locally by the caller, before this call, over the exact rotation payload this registrar independently reconstructs (same `operationalKeys`/`services`/`prev` shape `.../rotate` would build). This registrar can never produce that proof itself, since it will never hold `public_key`'s private half. A stale `prev` by the time the request arrives just fails the way any other `prev` mismatch does. Afterward, this registrar has overwritten its copy of the private key with a non-ciphertext sentinel -- not set it aside, not kept it for a future rotation, gone. Every row on this page except `.../take-custody` stops working for that identity from then on, with a clear error pointing at submitting pre-signed operations through §1 directly instead.

Refuses with a reason, unless `force: true` is set, when either is true: the identity has no current guardian at all (an unrecoverable identity the instant this key is lost, by anyone, ever), or a current guardian is also custodied by this registrar and alone satisfies `recovery_threshold` -- in that case this registrar can still rotate the identity's key at any time by signing as that guardian (REQ-7.2-1b carries no 72-hour window), so taking custody of the operational key doesn't fully remove this registrar from the identity's trust model. The bare-domain root identity can't call this at all -- it has to keep a key this registrar can read to sign every new registration's attestation.

## 3. Asynchronous signature collection (`pending_operations`)

For anything needing more than one signature collected over more than one request -- `guardian_add` against a non-empty guardian set (REQ-7.2-4), a forced `guardian_remove` (REQ-7.2-7b), `policy_update` (REQ-7.2-9), or a `guardian_relinquish`/guardian-initiated `custodial_rotate` whose required signers aren't all custodied by (or available in the same call to) this registrar.

Modeled as a state machine per pending proposal: `proposed -> collecting -> satisfied -> finalized`, with `expired` and `declined` as terminal alternatives. `finalized` is entered automatically the instant `satisfied` is reached (the registrar submits the now-complete operation to §1's own `/operations` itself) -- a caller never finalizes by hand.

A proposal can stay `collecting` for up to 7 days, long enough that a signer might rotate their own, unrelated operational key before everyone else has signed. This registrar records when it collected each signature and, at finalize time, verifies each one against whichever key its own signer held *then* (REQ-4-2) -- never against whatever's current by the time the last signature finally arrives. A signer rotating their own key mid-vote never invalidates a signature they already gave.

`decline` and `withdraw` are two distinct operations with different authority, not one action with a policy-configurable effect:

- **`decline` is a veto.** Any current, live guardian of the ward -- checked live, not just whoever this registrar's own advisory "required signers" guess happened to list -- can kill the proposal outright by declining, whether or not they'd already signed. Unconditional: it doesn't matter how many others had already approved. Allowed from `collecting` *or* `satisfied` (nothing is actually irreversible until it's truly in the log -- `satisfied` can still be sitting there unfinalized in the rare case a prior finalize attempt failed and is awaiting retry). Rejected once `finalized`/`declined`/`expired` -- none of those have an undo. One deliberate exception to "must already be a current guardian": `guardian_add`'s own `incoming` party can always decline a proposal naming them, live or not -- `guardianAddRule` (packages/lib) requires their own consent unconditionally, genesis or not, so the operation can never be satisfied without it regardless; declining your own nomination is a refusal, not an exercise of governance power over someone else's proposal, and it's the same single verb rather than a different one for that one case.
- **`withdraw` is a non-binding opt-out.** "Don't wait on me" -- removes the withdrawing party's own signature from consideration if they'd already contributed one, but never blocks anyone else from still reaching the threshold through some other combination. Only valid from `collecting` (once satisfied, nobody's waiting on anyone). A signer who withdrew can still change their mind and sign later; withdrawing isn't a lockout.

`decline`/`withdraw` accept two different kinds of proof, either is equally valid -- deliberately a *different*, simpler mechanism than `.../propose`/`.../sign`'s own operation-content proofs below, since declining or withdrawing is never itself an Operation appended to any ward's log:

- A **signed request** (`POST`, body `{signer_did, sig}`) -- `sig` is a plain, raw ECDSA signature (base64url, low-S) over the canonical payload `{action: "decline"|"withdraw", pending_operation_id: <id>}`, checked with `verifyPayload` directly against the signer's resolved key -- not a [Data Integrity proof](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-7), since this payload is never part of an Operation's own content. Works for anyone who can produce a signature, local or external to this registrar.
- A **token-based link** (`GET`, `?token=...`) -- the same trust model this registrar's own email-verification-link flow already uses: a random, unguessable token issued the first time a given signer is notified about a given proposal, usable by anyone who received it (possession of the verified email is the proof, not a signature). This is what makes the one-click links in the notification emails below work without needing browser-side cryptography, and it works for an externally-hosted guardian too -- the limiting factor was always whether this registrar has a verified way to reach them, never who custodies their key.

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `.../propose` | create a pending proposal for one operation type + its intended content, with the proposer's own proof attached if they're a required signer -- body is the partial operation itself, carrying a `proof` array exactly as [REQ-6-7](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-7) defines |
| `POST` | `.../pending/<id>/sign` | a required signer not yet counted adds their own proof -- body `{signer_did, proof}`, where `proof` is a single Data Integrity proof over the pending operation's own unsecured content (`GET .../pending/<id>`'s own `unsigned_payload`, below) |
| `POST` | `.../pending/<id>/sign-as-self` | `gw_session`-gated: signs server-side with the key this registrar already custodies for the logged-in identity, same model as `.../adopt`/`.../rotate` |
| `POST` or `GET` | `.../pending/<id>/decline` | veto -- POST with a signed or form body, or GET with `?token=...` |
| `POST` or `GET` | `.../pending/<id>/withdraw` | opt-out -- same proof options |
| `GET` | `.../pending/<id>` | content-negotiated: `Accept: text/html` renders the browser voting page below; anything else returns the same status JSON as always (required signers, who has signed, state) |
| `GET` | `/api/me/pending-signatures` | every pending proposal naming the caller as a required signer who hasn't yet signed |

A proposal not reaching `satisfied` within 7 days moves to `expired` -- always a failure, never an automatic pass; nothing in this method or this registrar advances a proposal just because time ran out. A required signer discovers a pending proposal by polling `/api/me/pending-signatures` or by email (§6) -- every state-moving event (propose, each signature, decline, withdraw, finalize) sends one, plus a daily reminder for anyone who still hasn't acted on a `collecting` proposal, explaining that consequence in plain terms.

**The browser voting page.** Every notification email links here (with a token, if one was issued) rather than to an action endpoint directly -- deliberately: an email client's own link-prefetching security scanner (Microsoft Safe Links, a corporate proxy, antivirus) visits a link the instant a message arrives, long before a person reads it, so a link that performed the action itself could be "voted" by the scanner, never by the person it was addressed to. The page shows state, required signers (with who's signed), and expiry, and -- only while `collecting` -- buttons that each `POST`:

- **Decline / Withdraw**, shown whenever a valid `?token=` is present in the URL -- the token itself is the proof, same as the API's own token path.
- **Sign**, shown only when the viewer is authenticated (§5's own `gw_session`) as a required signer who hasn't yet signed -- signing is held to a higher bar than decline/withdraw because it grants authority (e.g. a new guardian), so the email token alone isn't treated as sufficient; a logged-out viewer instead sees a link to §5's own login page. Only ever available for a locally-custodied identity, same limit every session-gated convenience endpoint already has.

## 4. Guardian deactivation policy

Entirely this registrar's own operational choice -- the formal spec (REQ-4-4) only requires that a deactivated guardian stop counting toward any threshold once its own `custodial_tombstone` lands; it says nothing about whether this registrar *accepts* that submission in the first place, or what else it does in response. Reused across both `.../tombstone` and any `pending_operations`-collected `custodial_tombstone` for a current guardian.

- **Acceptance**: this registrar's own configuration determines whether a `custodial_tombstone` for an identity that is still a current guardian of one or more wards is accepted outright, or rejected (directing the caller to first issue `guardian_remove`/`guardian_relinquish` against each ward it guards) -- a referential-integrity-style block, same spirit as a SQL foreign key.
- **Proactive handling (recommended over reactive, when the outgoing guardian is cooperating)**: this registrar *SHOULD* prefer to resolve `on_orphan: {"transfer_to": ...}` *before* a sole guardian's `custodial_tombstone` is even accepted -- the same add-then-remove discipline §7.2 of the formal spec's ordinary transfer already uses. While the outgoing guardian is still the ward's sole guardian, `guardian_add`'s non-empty-set rule (REQ-7.2-4) applies, not the harder zero-to-one one: `addition_threshold` evaluated at `N=1` is `majority = 1`, so the outgoing guardian's signature alone satisfies it. Sequencing `guardian_add(fallback)` then `guardian_remove(outgoing, voluntary)` *before* accepting the tombstone means the ward is never actually orphaned at any point, and the whole handoff only ever needs the outgoing guardian's key (plus the fallback's, trivial when it's this registrar's bare-domain root) -- the orphaned ward's operational key is never touched, exactly as easy as the `"tombstone"` case below. This is only available while the outgoing guardian is cooperatively initiating that tombstone request.
- **Reactive cascade, if offered**: when a ward's effective guardian set becomes empty with no opportunity for the proactive handling above to have run first -- a forced tombstone using a compromised key, or a sole guardian simply going unreachable without ever cooperating -- any automatic follow-up action this registrar takes on the affected ward's behalf *MUST* consult that ward's own `GuardianPolicy.min_guardian_count` and `on_orphan` (formal spec REQ-5-7/REQ-5-8) individually -- never one blanket behavior applied to every affected ward alike. If removing this guardian would leave a ward below its own `min_guardian_count`, that ward's own removal is refused even if the overall tombstone is otherwise accepted for the guardian's other wards. If it would leave a ward with zero guardians, that ward's own `on_orphan` states what this registrar should try to do next for it specifically, and the three values are not equally reachable in one call:
  - `"sovereign"` needs nothing further -- REQ-4-4's own exclusion already produces an empty guardian set from the existing log alone, no operation to construct.
  - `"tombstone"` needs a self-signed `custodial_tombstone` for the orphaned ward -- only ever needs *that ward's own* operational key (`tombstone_threshold` defaults to `any`, REQ-7.3-1), so this registrar can always do it unilaterally in the same call, provided it custodies that one ward's own key, with no dependency on any other party.
  - `{"transfer_to": ...}` now genuinely needs the harder zero-to-one `guardian_add` -- the proactive path above is no longer available, since the guardian set is already empty, so REQ-7.2-5 applies: *two* parties' keys together, the named DID's own consent and the orphaned ward's own key. Naming this registrar's own bare-domain root identity makes the first one trivial, but it still can't complete without the ward's own key too -- available in the same call only when the ward itself is also fully custodied here.

  Neither of the last two is ever something the library's own verification functions can produce on their own, regardless of policy -- both require this registrar to actually hold the signing key material behind at least one required signer. When any required signer's key isn't available in the same call, this registrar falls back to §3's own pending-operations collection instead of refusing outright -- proposing the operation with whichever signatures it can already supply, then waiting on the rest, same as any other multi-party operation; it may never complete if the missing signer is never reachable, same limitation §3 already has.
- **Creation-time policy defaults**: a field a creator leaves unset in `custodial_create`'s own optional `policy` resolves to the formal spec's own stated default (REQ-7.1-7, [REQ-5-10](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-5-10)) -- this registrar has no separate configured default of its own to fall back to instead, by design: a registrar-level override here was considered and specifically ruled out, so that two verifiers resolving the same unset field never disagree depending on which registrar they asked.

## 5. Login / OIDC

Two independent flows share the same underlying credential (`login_secret`) and the same `gw_session` cookie, for two different purposes:

- `/authorize`, `/token`, `/userinfo`, `/revoke`, `/oauth/register-client`, `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, `/.well-known/jwks.json` -- the OIDC relying-party flow, for a third-party application that wants to let someone sign in with their Guardian ID. See `packages/server/src/oidc.ts`.
- `GET`/`POST /guardian-login?return_to=<path>` -- this registrar's own first-party login, for this registrar's own pages (currently just §3's browser voting page). No client registration: it's just "sign in, then take me back to the same-origin path that sent me here" (`return_to` is restricted to a relative path -- no open redirect to an external target). See `votingPage.ts`.
- `POST /guardian-logout?return_to=<path>` -- ends the session: deletes the `login_sessions` row server-side (not just the cookie client-side, so the old session id can't be replayed) and clears the cookie. POST only, same reasoning as every other state-changing action here -- never a bare link a scanner could trigger. Linked from the account dashboard (§8).

Named `/guardian-login`/`/guardian-logout`, not the shorter `/login`/`/logout`, because a registrar is commonly deployed on a domain that already has its own, unrelated human-facing `/login` and `/logout` (many existing web apps already do). The two guardian-prefixed names don't share a route pattern with each other either -- `guardian-login` and `guardian-logout` diverge at their 13th character, so a prefix match on one never reaches the other; each needs its own wrangler route entry. Worth checking your own host application's routes before adding any new top-level path here, not just these two.

**A relying party's own `login_hint` always takes precedence over an already-active session.** `/authorize` compares a normalized `login_hint` against the current session's own name (the same normalization a login attempt itself goes through), and falls through to a login prompt -- pre-filled with the hint, same as having no session at all -- whenever they don't match, rather than silently proceeding as whoever happens to still be logged in.

**The bare-domain root identity logs in like any other ward**, once an operator has given it a credential (`ROOT_WARD_LOGIN_SECRET`, see the top-level README's self-hosting section) -- the name field on either login form accepts `_`, the bare registrar domain, `@<domain>`, or `_@<domain>`, all four resolving to the same identity. The last form matters in practice, not just for completeness: a relying party that forces a `name@domain` shape on its login form (Tailscale's custom-OIDC login does) leaves `_@<domain>` as the only way to reach the root identity through that form at all, since neither bare `_` nor bare `@<domain>` fits what the form demands. `normalizeLoginIdentifier` (login.ts) checks the *extracted* name against `"_"` rather than the raw, untrimmed input, so `_` survives having `@domain` sliced off after it, the same way a ward's name does. No self-service recovery if this password is lost -- see the README's section on resetting it directly against `wards.login_secret_hash`.

**`login_secret` can be either generated or user-chosen.** `POST /register` (§1) and this registrar's own registration page both offer a choice: let the registrar generate a high-entropy secret (the only option before this), or set a password instead (`{"name": "...", "password": "..."}` in the JSON body; a minimum length is enforced, no further composition rules). A generated secret is returned once, in the response, and never again; a chosen password is never echoed back, since the caller already knows it. Reissuing (`.../login-secret`, §2) takes the same optional `password` either way -- changing your own credential later works identically to setting it at registration.

### 5.1 Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591)

A relying party no longer needs this registrar's own operator to hand-insert an `oidc_clients` row -- `POST /oauth/register-client` is open, unauthenticated self-service, the same posture every other registration endpoint here already has:

```json {linenos=false}
{ "redirect_uris": ["https://app.example.com/callback"], "client_name": "Example App", "token_endpoint_auth_method": "client_secret_basic" }
```

Returns `client_id` (and `client_secret`, unless `token_endpoint_auth_method` was `"none"` -- a public client, e.g. a mobile app or SPA, which authenticates with PKCE alone), plus a `registration_access_token` for `GET /oauth/register-client/<client_id>` (RFC 7592's read operation; update/delete aren't implemented yet). Both the issued `client_secret` and `registration_access_token` are shown exactly once, at registration time, the same convention every other one-time secret in this registrar already follows.

### 5.2 Consent

`/authorize` shows an "*App X* wants access to -- Allow/Deny" screen before issuing a code, remembered per `(ward, client_id)` so a returning user isn't re-asked unless the requested `scope` actually grows. Denying redirects back with `?error=access_denied` and no code, per RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1.

### 5.3 PKCE

Mandatory for every client, confidential or public -- the OAuth 2.1 baseline. `/authorize` refuses to issue a code at all without a `code_challenge` (`S256` only); `/token` treats a stored code somehow missing one as a bug, not a legitimate case to fall back on.

### 5.4 Tokens, refresh, and revocation

The `authorization_code` grant now always returns a `refresh_token` alongside the access/id tokens (`id`/`access` tokens: 1 hour; refresh tokens: 30 days). `grant_type=refresh_token` rotates on every use -- the presented token is marked spent and a new one issued in its place, sharing the same underlying "family." Presenting an already-rotated-away token again (something a legitimate client never does) is treated as evidence of theft: the entire family is revoked, not just the one request denied.

`POST /revoke` (RFC 7009) takes `{ token, token_type_hint? }`. A refresh token is revoked directly; an access/id token (otherwise a stateless, unrevokable JWT) has its own `jti` added to a small blocklist that `/userinfo` checks going forward. Revocation is idempotent and always returns `200` regardless of whether the token was recognized, per RFC 7009 §2.2 -- never a way to probe which tokens exist.

Client authentication (where a client has a secret at all) accepts either `Authorization: Basic` or a `client_secret` body parameter, at both `/token` grant types.

### 5.5 `/userinfo` claims, and what's in the `id_token` itself

`/userinfo` always returns `sub`/`name`. `name` falls back to the bare registrar domain for the bare-domain root identity specifically, since its own `wards.name` is `""` (a sentinel, not a display name) and a literal empty string can fail a relying party's own validation -- the same fallback `agentCard.ts` already uses for this identity's display name elsewhere. `email`/`email_verified` are included only when the access token's own granted `scope` includes `email` *and* this identity has a verified forwarding address on file (§6) -- never invented, never returned for a scope that didn't ask for it. The root identity isn't excluded from this -- see §6's own note on how it gets a verifiable email address despite having no name-shaped local part.

**`email`'s own value is this ward's canonical `name@domain` -- never the forwarding address it happens to point mail at**, using `_` in place of a name for the bare-domain root specifically (§6). Those are two different facts: forwarding is where mail for this identity currently lands (an arbitrary, changeable third-party mailbox, never itself a second identity), while OIDC's `email` claim is supposed to assert something about *who the user is*. A relying party expecting its `login_hint` and the returned `email` to agree will otherwise see what looks like an identity mismatch, since the two addresses can differ by design. `email_verified: true` means this ward has confirmed, working forwarding configured (proof the identity is reachable by mail at all), not that the asserted `name@domain` address is itself a separately-verified mailbox. This also keeps a ward's actual forwarding destination private: it's this registrar's own notification system's business alone, and a relying party asking for the `email` scope learns the Guardian ID being signed in with, never where that identity's mail happens to land today. No `email` claim at all when forwarding isn't configured.

**`email`/`email_verified`, when present, are also duplicated directly into the `id_token`**, not only reachable via a separate `/userinfo` call. This is a deliberate compatibility choice, not spec-mandated (OIDC allows claims to live in either place) -- plenty of real-world relying parties, especially simpler "generic OIDC" integrations, only ever decode the `id_token` and never make a second `/userinfo` round trip. Same exact condition and same shared helper as `/userinfo`'s own check, not a duplicated logic path. Beyond those two claims, `id_token` stays minimal: `iss`, `sub` (the DID, not an email), `aud`, `iat`, `exp`, `nonce`, `jti` -- a relying party that auto-matches incoming SSO identities against existing user records by email or username, rather than accepting a bare DID as the subject, may still need that identity invited/mapped manually on its own side.

### 5.6 Finding the right registrar (discovery)

This is a client-side problem, not a missing endpoint -- a Guardian identifier already names its own registrar (`domain:name`), so an RP's own "Login with Guardian" button just needs to turn a person's `alice@acme.com`-shaped input into that domain's own `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, then redirect through the ordinary flow above. A minimal reference implementation:

```js {linenos=false}
async function loginWithGuardian(identifier, redirectUri) {
  const [name, domain] = identifier.split("@");
  const discovery = await fetch(`https://${domain}/.well-known/openid-configuration`).then((r) => r.json());
  const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
  const challenge = base64url(await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode(verifier)));
  sessionStorage.setItem("guardian_code_verifier", verifier); // survives the redirect round-trip
  const url = new URL(discovery.authorization_endpoint);
  url.search = new URLSearchParams({
    client_id: MY_CLIENT_ID, redirect_uri: redirectUri, response_type: "code",
    scope: "openid", code_challenge: challenge, code_challenge_method: "S256", login_hint: name,
  });
  location.href = url.toString();
}
```

`login_hint` (the standard OIDC authentication request parameter, already handled by `/authorize`) carries just the name part through to the registrar's own login form -- the person never has to type the domain part twice in two different shapes.

## 6. Email forwarding

`POST .../email` (set up forwarding), `GET /verify-email` (confirm a forwarding address). See `packages/server/src/email.ts`. Reused, not modified, by §3's own signer-notification need.

**The bare-domain root identity uses `_` as its reserved local part** (the same convention §5's login already uses) -- `_@<domain>` both addresses mail to it and is the value `email.ts` writes into `email_forwarding`, so inbound routing (name-keyed at the local part, per `handleEmail`) can find it the same way it finds any named ward. Root previously couldn't set up forwarding at all ("no local part to receive mail at"), which also meant it could never satisfy a relying party that hard-requires an `email` claim (§5.5) -- Tailscale's custom-OIDC login does. Once root has verified forwarding configured the same way a named ward does, its OIDC `email` claim becomes `_@<domain>`, verifiable like any other.

Outbound sending (the verification link itself, and every §3 notification) goes through `emailProviders.ts`. This registrar's own choice of provider is a deployment config, not a protocol or method detail: `EMAIL_PROVIDER` (a `wrangler.jsonc` var) names one of `mailchannels` | `resend` | `cloudflare-native` | `log` (dev-only -- prints instead of sending). Nothing here is specific to this provider list -- adding another is one more small function, never a reason to touch any caller. Unconfigured, outbound sending fails with a clear configuration error rather than a vendor-specific HTTP status.

Every provider except one is a plain `(apiKey, opts) -> Response` function using only `fetch`, no Workers-specific API, and that provider's own API key is set as a matching secret (`MAILCHANNELS_API_KEY`/`RESEND_API_KEY`) -- a self-hoster not on Cloudflare, or who'd rather not depend on a Workers-specific feature, picks one of these. `cloudflare-native` is the deliberate exception: Cloudflare's own native Email Sending binding (`send_email` in `wrangler.jsonc`), needing no external account or API key at all, just `wrangler email sending enable <domain>` once per domain (Cloudflare then manages the SPF/DKIM records itself) and the Workers Paid plan. guardianspec.org, the live instance this spec documents, uses it.

## 7. Login secret

Unchanged -- `POST .../login-secret` (reissue a lost or leaked one). See `packages/server/src/registrar.ts`'s `reissueLoginSecret`.

## 8. Account dashboard

Everything above this point is an API, consumed by a relying party's own code or an email client's link -- `GET /account` (after `/guardian-login`) is the one page where a person looks at and manages their own identity directly, the same first-party-HTML-page pattern §3's own voting page already established. See `packages/server/src/accountPage.ts`.

Shows identity status, current guardians and the effective `GuardianPolicy` thresholds, the full activity log, anything still waiting on this identity's own signature (linked to §3's voting page), and every connected OAuth app (§5.2's own consent records) with a "Revoke access" button that also kills any live refresh tokens for that app, not just the consent record -- revoking actually revokes, not just "stop remembering." A "Log out" button (§5's own `POST /guardian-logout`) sits at the top -- there was no way to end a session at all before this existed.

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/account` | the dashboard itself |
| `POST` | `/account/rotate` | rotate the operational key |
| `POST` | `/account/login-secret/reissue` | reissue the login secret (a generated one, shown once, same convention every other one-time secret here follows) -- or, given `password`/`password_confirm` fields instead, set your own password |
| `POST` | `/account/email` | set up forwarding (§6) |
| `POST` | `/account/relinquish` | relinquish all guardians |
| `GET`/`POST` | `/account/tombstone` | a confirmation page -- requires typing the account's own name, not a bare button -- then deactivates |
| `POST` | `/account/consents/revoke` | revoke a connected app's own access |

Every action here, including email forwarding, works for the domain's own bare-domain root identity too, the same as any named ward, once an operator has given it a login credential (see the top-level README's own self-hosting section) -- root uses `_` as its own reserved local part for forwarding (§6), the same convention §5's own login already established for it.

## 9. Managed Identity API

`POST /register` already exists for plain self-service -- this registrar's own profile convenience (§2), not the method-required `.../operations` path itself ([§1](#1-method-required-endpoints), formal spec [REQ-8-2](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-8-2)), though it produces exactly the same kind of guardian-less genesis either way. This section is about the one case that's different: an agent-hosting platform (zz's own managed-identity feature is the motivating example, not the only one) wants to create a *new* identity with a human as its own signed guardian from the moment it exists -- never ownerless, and never guarded by the platform itself.

**The guardian is derived from a validated access token's own `sub`, never a client-supplied field.** `POST /register` with `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` and a token whose own granted `scope` includes `create:managed-identity` creates the new ward with that token's own `sub` as its guardian. A request with no bearer token at all still gets the ordinary case: self-service, no guardian. A bearer token present but missing the scope is rejected outright (`403`), not silently downgraded to "no guardian."

This replaces an earlier gap: a `guardian_did` field in the request body, honored for any client that could authenticate with Basic auth (the same credential used at `/token`). Before dynamic client registration (§5.1) existed, that credential meant "a client the registrar operator hand-vetted" -- an implicit trust signal. Once registration became open and self-service, *any* caller could authenticate as *some* client and name *any other ward on this same registrar* as the guardian of a brand-new identity, with no verification that the named party ever consented -- a way to falsely imply a trust relationship (e.g. a new identity that looks vouched-for by a well-known account) that was never actually granted. Deriving the guardian from an access token closes this: the named guardian is always whoever the token proves is authenticated, and that person granted the scope explicitly, on the ordinary `/authorize` consent screen (§5.2) -- the same revocable consent every other scope already requires, not a client's own unverifiable say-so.

A platform wanting to use this needs its own OIDC client (§5.1) and a token for the acting human carrying `create:managed-identity` -- normally obtained the same way any other scope is, through that human's own `/authorize` consent. A client that only ever needs this occasionally can request it alongside `openid` at ordinary login time, store the resulting refresh token (§5.4), and mint a fresh access token on demand rather than redirecting through a fresh interactive consent on every single creation.

**The guardian's identity doesn't have to live on this same registrar.** A platform may legitimately onboard a human whose did:guardian identity is hosted elsewhere entirely -- their access token is then issued by *that* registrar, not this one, and a registrar can only verify a JWT signed with a key it actually holds. `FEDERATED_TRUSTED_ISSUERS` (an operator-configured, comma-separated allowlist of other registrar domains) opts this in explicitly: an access token whose `iss` matches a trusted peer is verified against *that peer's* `/.well-known/jwks.json` (fetched fresh, matched by `kid`), never assumed valid just because it claims a trusted domain. An issuer that's neither this registrar itself nor an explicitly trusted peer is rejected outright -- closed by default, the same posture every other access-control decision in this spec takes. `jti`-based revocation (§4) is only checked for this registrar's tokens; a federated peer's revocation state isn't visible here, the same limitation any JWT-based federation has without a shared introspection endpoint, bounded by the token's short TTL.

## 10. Delegation-chain tokens (token exchange)

A managed identity (§9) often needs to be *acted as* later, not just created once -- a platform letting its own user operate an agent it guards, say. `POST /token` with `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange` (RFC 8693) mints a token whose `sub` is a target identity (`resource`, a DID this registrar custodies), given a `subject_token` (the caller's own existing access token) proving who's actually asking:

```text {linenos=false}
POST /token
{
  "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange",
  "subject_token": "<the caller's own access token>",
  "resource": "did:guardian:acme.com:some-agent",
  "client_id": "...", "client_secret": "..."
}
```

**Authorization is the same live-guardian check used everywhere else a guardian's own standing matters** -- never a reimplementation: the caller (the `subject_token`'s own `sub`) must be `resource` itself, or a current, live guardian of it, checked fresh against `resource`'s own operation log every time (`@did-guardian/lib`'s own `liveGuardians`). Not a guardian, or not the identity itself: `403`. `resource` naming an identity this registrar doesn't custody fails too -- there's no key material to issue a token for it.

**The issued token carries `sub` = the target, and `act: { sub: <the caller's own DID> }`** -- the emerging OpenID on-behalf-of shape (`sub`/`act`), not a one-off: anything already built against that draft recognizes a token from this registrar unmodified. No `id_token` -- this isn't a fresh authentication event, just a scoped delegation of an already-authenticated caller's own, separately-proven authority. No refresh token either; the original `subject_token`'s own session is what covers re-exchange later.

## 11. A2A (Agent2Agent) interop

A2A's own Agent Card -- a JSON manifest advertising an identity's capabilities and how to authenticate with it -- is conventionally served at one fixed path per origin (`/.well-known/agent-card.json`), which doesn't fit this registrar's own multi-tenant shape: many identities under one domain. The fixed path stays correct for a single-agent origin; a still-individual-draft WebFinger discovery profile (`draft-zhao-a2a-webfinger-00`) covers exactly the multi-tenant case -- WebFinger is the discovery layer that resolves a *named* identity to wherever its own card actually lives, which doesn't have to be that fixed path.

- `GET /.well-known/agent-card.json` -- this domain's own bare-domain root identity (spec §2.1), satisfying A2A's own fixed-path convention for the one identity it actually fits here.
- `GET /.well-known/guardian/<name>/agent-card.json` -- a named ward's own card, at a path consistent with every other resolution this registrar already does.
- `GET /.well-known/webfinger?resource=acct:<name>@<domain>` -- resolves a named identity to its own card's URL (the JRD shape `draft-zhao-a2a-webfinger-00` itself specifies: `rel: "self"`, `type: "application/a2a+json"`).

Every card here declares `securitySchemes.oidc` (an `OpenIdConnectSecurityScheme` pointing at this registrar's own `/.well-known/openid-configuration`) -- how an A2A client authenticates with this identity is just this registrar's own OIDC flow, already documented in full above.

**The same WebFinger endpoint also serves OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0's unrelated WebFinger usage** -- `rel=http://openid.net/specs/connect/1.0/issuer` -- which is what a relying party that only has a user's identifier calls first, before ever fetching `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (e.g. a "log in with your identity provider" flow that takes `alice@guardianspec.org` directly, which is how Tailscale's custom-OIDC login discovers an issuer). The `href` returned is always the registrar's bare domain -- there's one OIDC issuer per registrar, not one per ward, so this step only ever confirms the identifier exists here at all. `rel` is a filter per RFC 7033: pass it zero or more times to get only matching links, or omit it to get every link this registrar knows for that resource (both the A2A one and the OIDC one, together).

**Deliberately unsigned in this pass.** A2A's own `AgentCardSignature` (JWS, canonicalized) is optional, not required -- plain HTTPS already gives a verifier a weaker binding to this domain. Signing with a ward's own operational key (already custodied here, already published in its own DID Document) is a natural fit for later, not something this first pass needed to block on.

## 12. MCP interop

MCP's own authorization spec is OAuth 2.1 plus mandatory Resource Indicators (RFC 8707) -- an MCP client treats the tool server it's calling as a *resource*, discovers who issues tokens for it, and asks for a token scoped to that one resource specifically, not a generic token good for anything the OAuth client happens to be. Two additions, both strictly additive -- every existing client that never sends a `resource` keeps getting exactly the behavior it already had.

**`GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`** (RFC 9728, Protected Resource Metadata): this registrar is both its own authorization server and, for endpoints like `/userinfo`, a protected resource in its own right. The document names itself as both:

```json {linenos=false}
{
  "resource": "https://acme.com",
  "authorization_servers": ["https://acme.com"],
  "bearer_methods_supported": ["header"],
  "scopes_supported": ["openid", "email", "create:managed-identity"]
}
```

A `401` from `/userinfo` (missing, invalid, expired, or revoked token) carries a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://acme.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"` header (RFC 9728 §5.1) -- a generic client discovers the authorization server from the 401 alone, with nothing hardcoded out of band.

**`resource` at `/authorize` and `/token`** (RFC 8707 Resource Indicators): a client naming a `resource` (an absolute URI, no fragment -- e.g. the MCP tool server's own URL) at `/authorize` gets an access token whose `aud` is that URI instead of the OAuth client's own `client_id` -- the resource server checks a token meant for *it*, not evidence that *some* client authenticated. A refresh request may narrow which resource a fresh token is scoped to, but never introduce one that wasn't already established at the original `/authorize` -- a client that never asked for resource scoping can't add it later through refresh alone.

## 13. Cross-registrar signature relay

§3 noted in passing that for a foreign required signer, "the limiting factor was always whether this registrar has a verified way to reach them, never who custodies their key." This section closes that gap for a fully custodial guardian -- one whose private key lives server-side on their own registrar and is never exposed to them, so they can't produce a raw signature the way a self-held-key external guardian can via `.../pending/<id>/sign` directly.

**The problem this solves.** `guardian_add` against an empty guardian set, when `incoming` is hosted on a different registrar (REQ-7.2-5), already falls back to §3's own pending-operations collection -- the ward's registrar proposes the operation and waits correctly. But the guardian's own registrar previously had no way to know that proposal existed at all (its own notification email lookup finds nothing, since email forwarding is set up per-registrar and this guardian isn't a local ward here), and even if told by hand, had no mechanism to produce a signature on the guardian's behalf. Entirely additive: no change to any existing endpoint's own behavior, no new crypto, no new federation configuration.

**`POST /.well-known/guardian/relay-notify`** -- a best-effort, advisory push from a ward's registrar to a required signer's own registrar, sent alongside every ordinary `notifyAwaitingSignature`/`notifyProgress` email for a signer this registrar doesn't custody:

```json {linenos=false}
{ "ward_did": "did:guardian:acme.com:alice", "pending_operation_id": "<id>", "signer_did": "did:guardian:otherdomain.com:bob" }
```

Never trusted blindly. The receiving registrar only ever uses this to independently re-fetch the current status from `GET .../pending/<id>` on the *ward's* own registrar (the same no-auth, read-only endpoint §3 already documents) before acting -- confirming the operation is still `collecting` or `satisfied`, and `signer_did` is genuinely a required signer who hasn't already signed. If `signer_did` isn't a local ward here, or the independent fetch fails or doesn't confirm, this silently no-ops. A caller whose peer doesn't implement this endpoint at all, or is simply unreachable, loses nothing beyond the proactive notification -- the ward can still share the pending-op link by hand, the same fallback that's always existed.

`GET .../pending/<id>`'s own JSON response (§3) now additionally carries `unsigned_payload`: the operation with every `proof` entry stripped, exactly the content a signer's own proof needs to be computed over. Not new information in principle -- a pending operation's own existence and required signers were never secret -- just not previously exposed in machine-usable form.

**`GET`/`POST /relay-sign`** -- the guardian's own review page, on *their* registrar, `gw_session`-gated like every other session-scoped convenience endpoint. `GET /relay-sign?ward=<ward_did>&op=<id>` fetches the live status from the ward's registrar, confirms the logged-in identity is actually a required signer, and shows the operation type, ward, and full payload for review. Two actions from there, `POST`ed back to the same page (same query parameters as form fields) and re-verified server-side on every one -- nothing from the `GET` is ever trusted:

- **Approve & sign** -- signs with `decryptWardPrivateKey` + `createProof`, the identical pair `.../sign-as-self` (§2) already uses for same-registrar operations, producing a Data Integrity proof over `unsigned_payload` above, and submits the result (`{signer_did, proof}`) to the ward registrar's own `.../pending/<id>/sign`. That endpoint's own proof verification (§3, against the signer's own resolved key) is completely unchanged -- a forged or buggy relay notification can waste an email or fail a submission, never cause a wrongly-satisfied operation.
- **Decline** -- signs `{ action: "decline", pending_operation_id }` and submits it to the ward registrar's existing `.../pending/<id>/decline`, which already accepts a signed body from anyone who can produce a valid signature over it (§3's `resolveActor`) -- the exact mechanism a local guardian's own decline already uses. An authoritative decline, never a local dismiss: it always blocks the proposal, whether as a current guardian's veto or, per §3's own documented exception, as a `guardian_add`'s own `incoming` party refusing their own nomination -- one verb rather than a different one (withdraw) for a case that was already functionally equivalent to a veto for that op type.

A decline relayed this way always reaches a terminal `declined` state on the ward's own registrar, not just the signer's registrar's local view of it.

**Persistent inbox for incoming relay requests.** A durable `relay_inbox` row (one per signer + pending operation, upserted on every `relay-notify`) exists independently of whether the one-shot notification email ever lands. The account dashboard (§8) shows it as its own "Needs your signature (another registrar)" section, alongside the existing local one. This is an index for discovery only, never a cache of truth -- opening any entry still always re-fetches the live status from the ward's own registrar first, the same as it always has; the row is marked resolved once *this* registrar has actually signed or declined on the signer's behalf, not before.

## 14. Registration modes and the admin console

This registrar's own public instance (guardianspec.org) runs **open**: anyone can `POST /register` and create an account, the behavior documented in §1. A different operator -- someone who controls the whole domain, personally or as a business, and wants their own root identity (§2.1 of the formal spec) usable everywhere did:guardian/did:web is accepted without exposing that same open door publicly -- instead runs **closed** (`REGISTRATION_MODE=closed`, a `vars` entry in `wrangler.jsonc`, not a secret).

Closed mode blocks only *anonymous* self-service at `/register` -- a bare name with no prior authorization, at all three of its branches (the browser form, the JSON API without a bearer token, and the registration page itself, which shows a plain "registration is closed" message instead of the form). A Managed Identity API bearer token (§9, `create:managed-identity` scope) still works either way, since that caller is already authenticated by a scope-checked token -- in a closed deployment such a token could only ever have come from someone who already has an account there, i.e. one the operator created.

**The admin console** (`GET /admin`, `GET`/`POST /admin/create-account`) is how a closed deployment's own operator creates those accounts -- for other people or for agents they manage. Available on every deployment regardless of `REGISTRATION_MODE`; gated to a `gw_session` resolved to the root identity specifically, the same `wards.name === ""` sentinel §2.1 and `ROOT_WARD_LOGIN_SECRET` (README.md) already establish -- no separate role or permission system.

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/admin` | lists every account on this registrar (name, DID, created-at) |
| `GET`/`POST` | `/admin/create-account` | the same generated-secret-or-set-your-own-password choice `/register` offers (§1), plus an optional `guardian_did` -- `registerWard`'s own existing param, the same one the Managed Identity API already uses, so an admin can name an initial guardian (e.g. themselves) at creation time instead of adding one later |

**v1 scope.** The admin console lists and creates; it doesn't let the root identity view, rotate, or tombstone *someone else's* account -- a bigger question (impersonation/management scope) left for its own future discussion. No claim-link credential flow -- an admin-created account's own owner changes their password any time afterward through the ordinary account dashboard (§8), the same action available to any self-registered account.

## Changelog

- **2026-11-22**: corrected §4's creation-time policy defaults description -- it previously described a registrar-configurable default `GuardianPolicy` this registrar never actually implemented (always just the formal spec's own stated defaults, re-exported as `DEFAULT_GUARDIAN_POLICY`), and which the formal spec now explicitly rules out ([REQ-5-10](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-5-10)) regardless.
- **2026-11-22**: `.../log-head` is now listed in §1's method-required table, not described as this registrar's own convenience -- [REQ-8-2](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-8-2) now requires it from every conformant registrar, not just this one. Its `sig` field (raw base64url) is replaced with `proof`, a single W3C Data Integrity proof, matching [REQ-6-7](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#req-6-7)'s format like every other signature in this method.
- **2026-11-21**: updated for [the method spec's own coordinated security rewrite](/docs/did-guardian-spec-v0.2.0/#changelog) (Fixes 1-7, same date): `.../take-custody`'s body is now `{public_key, key_proof, force?}` (a Data Integrity proof of possession, not a raw `key_sig`); `.../pending/<id>/sign`'s body is now `{signer_did, proof}`; `.../log-head`'s shape gained `logHash`; the cross-registrar relay's `unsigned_payload` and its approve-and-sign path now work in terms of Data Integrity proofs rather than raw signatures. `decline`/`withdraw`'s own raw-signature mechanism (§3) is unchanged by any of this -- that payload was never part of an Operation's own signed content to begin with.

Fixes made while integrating this registrar with third-party OIDC relying parties (Tailscale's custom-OIDC login, specifically), kept here rather than narrated inline in the sections above:

- `/authorize` previously let an already-active session from a different login silently continue into a new relying-party flow, with no check against what that flow actually requested -- surfaced as a confusing identity-mismatch error on the relying party's own side. Fixed by comparing `login_hint` against the current session (§5).
- `normalizeLoginIdentifier` checked the raw login input against `"_"` instead of the name extracted after slicing off `@domain`, so `_@<domain>` -- the only login form some relying parties' own forms allow for the root identity -- didn't resolve. Fixed (§5).
